planting.note: Sow into a gritty, mineral-heavy mix with almost no organic matter and give young plants a genuine cold, dry winter rest, since this Colorado Plateau slickrock native needs winter chill to flower reliably and rots quickly in damp conditions.

directions: Whipple fishhook cactus roots directly into thin pockets of sand and grit atop bare sandstone benches, slickrock ledges, and petrified dune outcrops across the Four Corners region, where little else can establish. The squat, ribbed body carries densely packed areoles with one or more stout, strongly hooked central spines, giving the whole plant a bristly, armored look even before it blooms. In mid-spring, funnel-shaped flowers in lavender-pink to magenta open near the crown, followed by small dry fruit. Specialty cactus growers propagate it from seed in a lean, fast-draining mix and withhold water almost entirely once cold weather sets in, since this species depends on a dry dormancy to avoid rot.

planting.note: Direct-sow seed in fall onto lean, rocky or gravelly soil so winter moisture and freeze-thaw cycles work it into crevices; rock goldenrod wedges itself into bare sandstone cracks and rimrock ledges rather than open ground.

directions: Rock goldenrod forms a low, woody-based clump of narrow, resinous, gray-green leaves that wedge into thin sandstone cracks and rimrock ledges across the Colorado Plateau and Great Basin, surviving on almost no soil. Dense, flat-topped clusters of small bright-yellow, goldenrod-like flower heads open in late summer, well after most other dryland rock garden plants have finished, making it a valuable late-season nectar source. It spreads very slowly from a persistent woody base rather than running, so it stays tidy among rock crevices or gravel mulch for years. Keep it on lean, mineral soil in full sun; rich soil or regular watering causes it to sprawl and rot.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring, tucking roots into pockets of sand or grit between bare sandstone slabs; this Four Corners slickrock native needs almost no supplemental water once rooted.

directions: Bailey's yucca is a small, stemless, clump-forming species rooted directly into cracks and thin sand pockets on bare slickrock benches and petrified-dune sandstone across the Four Corners region, where it tolerates extreme heat, reflected glare, and near-total drought. Its narrow, rigid, blue-green leaves carry curling white marginal fibers and a sharp terminal spine, forming a tighter, more southerly counterpart to the better-known Harriman's yucca of the higher Colorado Plateau. A stout flower stalk rises a foot or two above the foliage in early summer, carrying pendulous, creamy-white bell flowers. Propagate by dividing offsets from the base of an established clump and set them into sharply drained, mineral soil in full sun.

planting.note: Direct-sow after the last frost into sandy or gravelly, lean soil in full sun on open, bare ground typical of slickrock benches and petrified-dune flats; established plants reseed readily in undisturbed gravel.

directions: Navajo tea is a slender, almost leafless wildflower of sandy and gravelly slickrock flats and petrified-dune soils across the Colorado Plateau, sending up wiry stems topped with simple, rayless or sparsely rayed yellow flower heads through summer. Its thread-like foliage and open, airy habit let it slip into gravel beds and bare rock gardens without competing for root space. Long valued by Navajo and other regional communities, the dried flowering stems are steeped into a mild, reddish herbal tea, and the plant is still grown today for that traditional use as well as for xeriscape wildflower plantings. Give it full sun and lean, fast-draining soil; it declines quickly in rich garden beds or with regular irrigation.
